fanoutqa_039368.t: Douglas Diamond :: The Diamond–Dybvig Model :: chunk_0002
fanoutqa_039368.x:
Douglas Diamond :: The Diamond–Dybvig Model :: chunk_0002
The Diamond–Dybvig model, first introduced in the *Journal of Political Economy* in 1983, remains one of the most influential frameworks in modern banking theory.[[15]](#cite_note-15) The model demonstrates how banks engage in liquidity transformation by using short-term deposits from savers to fund long-term lending activities. This maturity mismatch makes banks vulnerable to runs if large numbers of depositors simultaneously demand their funds. Diamond and Dybvig show that government-provided deposit insurance can prevent self-fulfilling bank runs by assuring depositors that their funds are safe.

The model has become a foundational tool for academic research in banking, macroeconomics, and financial stability. Its insights have strongly influenced governmental and central bank policy, particularly in the design and justification of deposit insurance systems and liquidity regulations around the world. Following the global financial crisis of 2008, the framework provided theoretical support for liquidity backstops, emergency lending facilities, and stricter oversight of banks’ balance sheets.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

In recent years, researchers have extended the Diamond–Dybvig model to analyze runs in nonbank financial institutions, including money market mutual funds and cryptocurrency exchanges, where similar liquidity mismatches exist.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

The team last played in the NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament in 2025. The Cougars are currently coached by [Kelvin Sampson](/wiki/Kelvin_Sampson "Kelvin Sampson"). The Cougars play their home games in the [Fertitta Center](/wiki/Fertitta_Center "Fertitta Center"), which opened during the 2018–19 season after renovation of the former Hofheinz Pavilion. During the renovation, home games were played at [H&PE Arena](/wiki/Health_and_Physical_Education_Arena "Health and Physical Education Arena") at [Texas Southern University](/wiki/Texas_Southern_University "Texas Southern University").

Cynthia Lummis :: Early life and education :: chunk_0002
Cynthia Marie Lummis was born on September 10, 1954, in [Cheyenne, Wyoming](/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming "Cheyenne, Wyoming"), to Doran Lummis and Enid Bennett. She is descended from German immigrants; her family first came to Wyoming in 1868. Her father chaired the [Laramie County Republican Party](/wiki/Laramie_County,_Wyoming "Laramie County, Wyoming") and served on the county board of commissioners. Her brother Del Lummis also chaired the Laramie County Republican Party.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Lummis attended [Cheyenne East High School](/wiki/Cheyenne_East_High_School "Cheyenne East High School"), and graduated from the [University of Wyoming](/wiki/University_of_Wyoming "University of Wyoming") with a [Bachelor of Science](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [animal science](/wiki/Animal_science "Animal science") in 1976 and a Bachelor of Science in [biology](/wiki/Biology "Biology") in 1978.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) She graduated from the University of Wyoming with a [Juris Doctor](/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") in 1985, and was on the [dean's list](/wiki/Dean%27s_list "Dean's list").[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) She worked as a [student teacher](/wiki/Student_teacher "Student teacher") at Rock River School in 1977.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

William was educated at [private schools](/wiki/Private_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom "Private schools in the United Kingdom"). He started at Jane Mynors' nursery school and the pre-preparatory [Wetherby School](/wiki/Wetherby_School "Wetherby School"), both in London, before continuing at [Ludgrove School](/wiki/Ludgrove_School "Ludgrove School") near [Wokingham](/wiki/Wokingham "Wokingham"), Berkshire.[[33]](#cite_note-36)[[34]](#cite_note-37) At Ludgrove, he was active in sport before being admitted to [Eton College](/wiki/Eton_College "Eton College"), where he studied geography, biology, and history of art at [A-Level](/wiki/A-Level "A-Level"), and took part in several sports.[[35]](#cite_note-38)[[36]](#cite_note-39)

The decision to send William to Eton broke with royal tradition, as his father and grandfather had both attended [Gordonstoun](/wiki/Gordonstoun "Gordonstoun").[[37]](#cite_note-40) The royal family and the press agreed that William would be allowed to study free from media intrusion in exchange for periodic official updates.[[38]](#cite_note-41) In June 1991, he was admitted to the [Royal Berkshire Hospital](/wiki/Royal_Berkshire_Hospital "Royal Berkshire Hospital") after being accidentally hit on the forehead by a fellow pupil wielding a golf club. He suffered a depressed fracture of the skull and underwent surgery at [Great Ormond Street Hospital](/wiki/Great_Ormond_Street_Hospital "Great Ormond Street Hospital"), leaving a permanent scar.[[39]](#cite_note-university-42) The incident received widespread media attention.[[40]](#cite_note-rbarber-43)

After leaving Eton, William took a gap year. He joined [British Army](/wiki/British_Army "British Army") training exercises in Belize,[[41]](#cite_note-BBCBelize-44) worked on English dairy farms, and visited Africa. fanoutqa_001992.t: Epidemiology of cancer :: Rates and mortality :: Incidence of a second cancer in survivors :: chunk_0007
fanoutqa_001992.x:
Epidemiology of cancer :: Rates and mortality :: Incidence of a second cancer in survivors :: chunk_0007
In 2003, in the developed world, one in three people developed cancer during their lifetimes. If all cancer patients survived and cancer occurred randomly, the normal lifetime odds of developing a second primary cancer (not the first cancer spreading to a new site) would be one in nine.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) However, [cancer survivors](/wiki/Cancer_survivor "Cancer survivor") have an increased risk of developing a second primary cancer, and the odds in 2003 were about one in 4.5.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) About half of these second primaries can be attributed to the normal one-in-nine risk associated with random chance.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31)

The increased risk is believed to be primarily due to the same risk factors that produced the first cancer, such as the person's genetic profile, alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, and environmental exposures, and partly due, in some cases, to the treatment for the first cancer, which might have included mutagenic chemotherapeutic drugs or radiation.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31) Cancer survivors may be more likely to comply with recommended screening, and may be more likely than average to detect cancers.[[31]](#cite_note-Rheingold03-31)

The first Premier League goal was scored by [Brian Deane](/wiki/Brian_Deane "Brian Deane") of [Sheffield United](/wiki/Sheffield_United_F.C. "Sheffield United F.C.") in a 2–1 win against Manchester United.[[37]](#cite_note-39)

Manchester United won the inaugural edition of the new league, ending a twenty-six year wait to be crowned champions of England. Bolstered by this breakthrough, United quickly became the dominant force in the Premier League, winning seven of the first nine titles and securing two League and FA Cup doubles. They were initially led by experienced players such as [Bryan Robson](/wiki/Bryan_Robson "Bryan Robson"), [Steve Bruce](/wiki/Steve_Bruce "Steve Bruce"), [Paul Ince](/wiki/Paul_Ince "Paul Ince"), [Mark Hughes](/wiki/Mark_Hughes "Mark Hughes") and [Eric Cantona](/wiki/Eric_Cantona "Eric Cantona"), before evolving into a younger, more dynamic side featuring [Roy Keane](/wiki/Roy_Keane "Roy Keane") and the [Class of 92](/wiki/Fergie%27s_Fledglings "Fergie's Fledglings"), a group of homegrown talents including [David Beckham](/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") and [Paul Scholes](/wiki/Paul_Scholes "Paul Scholes").

At the end of the 1994–95 season, four rather than three clubs were relegated, while only two were promoted from the Football League First Division. This allowed the Premier League to reduce its size from 22 to 20 clubs for the start of the [1995–96](/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_FA_Premier_League "1995–96 FA Premier League") season, reducing the number of matches per team from 42 to 38.

Between 1993 and 1997, [Blackburn Rovers](/wiki/Blackburn_Rovers_F.C. "Blackburn Rovers F.C.") and [Newcastle United](/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") came closest to challenging United's early dominance. Further information: [List of Brown University buildings](/wiki/List_of_Brown_University_buildings "List of Brown University buildings")

Brown's main campus, comprises 235 buildings and 143 acres (58 ha) in the [East Side](/wiki/East_Side,_Providence,_Rhode_Island "East Side, Providence, Rhode Island") neighborhood of College Hill. The university's central campus sits on a 15-acre (6.1 ha) block bounded by Waterman, Prospect, George, and [Thayer Streets](/wiki/Thayer_Street "Thayer Street"); newer buildings extend northward, eastward, and southward. Brown's core, historic campus, constructed primarily between 1770 and 1926, is defined by three greens: the Front or Quiet Green, the Main or College Green, and the Ruth J. Simmons Quadrangle (historically known as Lincoln Field).[[63]](#cite_note-campus_heritage2-68)[[64]](#cite_note-69) A brick and wrought-iron fence punctuated by decorative gates and arches traces the block's perimeter. This section of campus is primarily [Georgian](/wiki/Georgian_architecture "Georgian architecture") and [Richardsonian Romanesque](/wiki/Richardsonian_Romanesque "Richardsonian Romanesque") in its architectural character.[[63]](#cite_note-campus_heritage2-68)

To the south of the central campus are academic buildings and residential quadrangles, including Wriston, Keeney, and Gregorian quadrangles. Immediately to the east of the campus core sit Sciences Park and Brown's [School of Engineering](/wiki/Brown_University_School_of_Engineering "Brown University School of Engineering"). North of the central campus are performing and visual arts facilities, life sciences labs, and the Pembroke Campus, which houses both dormitories and academic buildings. Facing the western edge of the central campus sit two of the Brown's seven libraries, the [John Hay Library](/wiki/John_Hay_Library "John Hay Library") and the [John D.
